criteria.note: The keyword intent — how to read a Korean food label for gluten — is answered concretely within the first ~60 words by naming 밀 and the flip-and-scan action, before any preamble.
Title is 38 chars (58 with the ' | Gluten-Free Korea' suffix), description is ~153 chars, keyword terms appear in both, and the phrasing does not repeat between them.

Headings carry the argument on their own: skimming Step 1–4 plus 'When the label can't answer', 'Three Korea-specific gluten-label traps' and 'What actually passes' reconstructs the full method and its limits.

Six internal links across four destinations, each placed where the reader would actually want the handoff (low-gluten trap → hidden-gluten guide, flavour detail → snack guide, soy-sauce marinade → condiments).
All three FAQ answers are fully established by the body — the 별표 2 wheat-only scope, the 쌀 marketing trap, and the full 밀/소맥/보리/엿기름/맥아/호밀 vocabulary table all appear verbatim in the article.

There is real first-hand signal — a self-corrected error, the habit narrative, shopping in Seoul — but the observations are concrete-but-thin: no product names, store names, dates, or counts attached to what was actually scanned.
criteria.evidence_quote: Everything about what sits on convenience-store shelves is our own shopping in Seoul — first-hand, but not a survey, and not lab-tested.

criteria.note: Korean terms are consistently given with Hangul plus romanisation in a checkable table, and figures and product identifiers (고시 제2025-60호, 별표 2, 포카칩 오리지널, 양조간장 501) are precise enough to verify.
Primary sources are linked with notice numbers and dates — the MFDS standard as 고시 제2025-60호, 29 August 2025, plus Sempio and Orion manufacturer product pages each marked 'retrieved August 2026'.
The piece states plainly what its method cannot establish and flags unverified glosses, and there are no affiliate or commercial links to disclose.

findings.quote: The snack that broke me of trusting the allergen line alone was a "rice" cracker: allergen line clean, but 밀 전분 sitting a few items up in the ingredients.
findings.why: This is the article's strongest first-hand failure story, but it carries no brand, product name, store chain, or date — so it reads as an anecdote rather than a verifiable observation, and it sits in a piece that elsewhere names 포카칩 오리지널 and Sempio 양조간장 501 precisely.
findings.fix: Name the cracker brand/product and roughly when and where it was bought (e.g. 'a CU-shelf 쌀과자 from [brand], March 2026'), and add one or two more dated shelf observations — how many of the ~N convenience-store items you scanned actually cleared.

findings.quote: A: Flip the package and read the ingredient list (원재료명, wonjaeryomyeong). Korea's mandatory allergen list — set by the MFDS labeling standard 식품등의 표시기준, 별표 2 — includes wheat, so wheat shows up as 밀.
findings.why: Every claim in this answer is supported by the body, but the answer runs well past the length Google renders in an FAQ rich result, so the parts that matter most for celiac readers (the shared-facility caveat, the 소비자상담실 fallback) will be truncated away.
findings.fix: Trim FAQ 1 to roughly 300 characters — lead with the 원재료명 + 밀/보리/호밀 scan and the 'clean list ≠ no trace gluten' limit — and move the MFDS notice detail into the body only, where it already lives.

findings.quote: We have not found a Korean equivalent of GFCO — a third-party scheme that audits a facility and licenses a seal — so a front-label claim in Korea is not backed by the outside verification a GFCO mark implies.
findings.why: Not a scoring problem — the hedge is properly framed as a limit of the authors' search rather than a fact — but it is an absence claim about a national certification landscape resting entirely on the authors' own failure to find one, which is the kind of statement most likely to age badly.
findings.fix: Add a one-line note on what was actually searched (e.g. 'checked MFDS 건강기능식품/표시 schemes and KFDA certification marks as of August 2026') so a reader can judge how thorough the negative finding is.

criteria.note: Regulatory claims carry a linked standard with notice number and retrieval date, manufacturer claims carry product-page links, and every shelf-level generalisation is explicitly flagged as the authors' own shopping ('On the shelves we scan', 'where we've been caught most often', 'we haven't verified either per product').

Product names, allergen lists, notice number, and dates are all specific and checkable, and internally consistent (frontmatter date Thu 30 Jul 2026 is a real Thursday; the 'Updated August 2026' note matches the 엿기름 correction described in the body).

A dedicated 'Where the claims here come from' paragraph separates the regulatory reading from first-hand shopping and states what the latter is not ('not a survey, and not lab-tested'), and 'Clears the scan' is defined as a label reading rather than a classification.

No absolute safety claim anywhere; cross-contamination gets its own step plus the asymmetry that a blank line is weak evidence, and celiac is given the stricter branch every time it diverges from NCGS.

The MFDS notice is dated and its amendment risk flagged ('check the notice number against the one in force when you read this'), manufacturer pages carry 'retrieved August 2026', and reformulation drift gets a standing caution.

The load-bearing fact is correct and correctly applied — wheat is a designated allergen, barley and rye are not — and 원재료명, 알레르기 유발물질, 영양성분, 혼합제제, 소비자상담실, and the 소맥/엿기름/맥아 glosses are all described accurately with sound romanisation.

The reader gets the primary law link, the manufacturer pages, the 식품안전나라 database, and a copy-pasteable Korean question for the consumer line — enough to check every safety-relevant claim without trusting the author.

findings.quote: **"글루텐프리" is self-declared.** With no Korean equivalent of a GFCO-style third-party audit that we've been able to find, a front-label gluten-free claim tells you what the manufacturer says, not what an outside body checked.
findings.why: Literally true and erring conservative, so no reader is put at risk. But it is an incomplete picture of Korean law: MFDS sets a numeric ceiling for products carrying a gluten-free claim, so the claim is self-declared against a legal threshold rather than being purely the maker's word. A reader who later learns this may conclude the article overstated its scepticism and discount its other regulatory statements.
findings.fix: Add one clause distinguishing the two ideas: the claim is regulated as to content (a legal maximum gluten level applies) but not third-party audited as to facility. Cite the threshold from the same MFDS standard already linked, or state plainly that the piece has not verified the threshold provision.

findings.quote: The **Onion flavour of the same brand declares 밀.**
findings.why: The preceding link is anchored to the Original's product page (goodsno=26). The Onion claim is bolded and carries the article's central lesson, but a reader following the link may not land on the page that substantiates it. The direction of error is safe — a reader avoids a chip that may be fine — so this does not affect a safety decision and no point is withheld.
findings.fix: Link the Onion flavour's own product page, or state that both flavours' allergen declarations appear on the same Orion listing, so the reader can confirm the contrast in one click.
